subject: science
title: US Middle School Science — Water Cycle and Oceans
subtitle: Reading passages about water-cycle and ocean-system interactions.
description: Five source-grounded reading passages test retrieval, inference, data reasoning, and explanation about water, oceans, currents, human impacts, and scientific evidence.

data.sourceTitle: Earth’s Water as a Connected System
data.targetTitle: Earth’s Water as a Connected System
data.sourcePassage: Earth’s water moves through a connected system that includes oceans, atmosphere, land, ice, groundwater, and living things. Most of Earth’s water is salty ocean water, while only a small amount is fresh water that people can use easily. Water can be stored in reservoirs such as oceans, glaciers, lakes, rivers, and aquifers. It can also move between spheres. For example, water evaporates from the hydrosphere into the atmosphere, falls as precipitation, infiltrates into the geosphere, and is taken up by plants in the biosphere. Because the parts are connected, a change in one part can affect many others. A long drought can lower soil moisture, reduce river flow, stress plants and animals, and slow groundwater recharge.

questions.question: Where is most of Earth’s water found?
questions.modelAnswer: Most of Earth’s water is salty ocean water.

questions.question: Name two reservoirs where water can be stored.
questions.modelAnswer: Water can be stored in reservoirs such as oceans, glaciers, lakes, rivers, and aquifers.

questions.question: How can water move from the hydrosphere to the atmosphere?
questions.modelAnswer: Water can evaporate from liquid water into water vapor in the atmosphere.

questions.question: Why can a drought affect more than one part of Earth’s system?
questions.modelAnswer: Because the system is connected, drought can reduce soil moisture, river flow, plant water, animal water, and groundwater recharge.

questions.question: Which statement best describes a system?
questions.modelAnswer: A system is a group of connected parts that interact and affect one another.
options: A group of connected parts that interact
A single object with no connections

data.sourcePassage: The Sun is the main energy source for the water cycle. When liquid water gains enough energy, some molecules escape from the surface and become invisible water vapor. This process is evaporation. Evaporation can happen at many temperatures, not only when water boils. Warm temperatures, wind, and dry air can increase evaporation. When warm, moist air rises, it cools. Cooler air cannot hold as much water vapor, so some vapor condenses into tiny liquid droplets or ice crystals. These droplets and crystals make clouds visible because they scatter light. Clouds are not made of invisible water vapor alone. Inside clouds, droplets can combine and ice crystals can grow. When they become heavy enough, gravity pulls them down as precipitation.

questions.question: What is the main energy source for the water cycle?
questions.modelAnswer: The Sun is the main energy source.

questions.question: What is evaporation?
questions.modelAnswer: Evaporation is liquid water changing into invisible water vapor.

questions.question: Which condition can increase evaporation?
questions.modelAnswer: Warm temperature, wind, or dry air can increase evaporation.

questions.question: Why are clouds visible if water vapor is invisible?
questions.modelAnswer: Clouds are visible because they contain tiny liquid droplets or ice crystals that scatter light.

questions.question: Explain how the Sun and gravity work together in this passage.
questions.modelAnswer: The Sun provides energy for evaporation and cloud formation, while gravity pulls heavy droplets or ice particles down as precipitation.

data.sourcePassage: After precipitation reaches land, water can follow several pathways. Some water flows over the surface as runoff. Some collects in rivers, lakes, or oceans. Some infiltrates into soil and rock, where it can become groundwater. Groundwater moves slowly through small spaces and cracks and may be stored in aquifers. Aquifers can supply wells, springs, wetlands, rivers, and lakes, but they may recharge slowly. Surface cover affects how much runoff forms. Pavement is mostly impermeable, so water cannot easily pass through it. Grass-covered soil is more permeable and can allow more infiltration. In cities, heavy rain can overwhelm storm drains, especially where there are many paved surfaces. Solutions such as rain gardens, permeable pavement, wetlands, and trees can reduce runoff and support local ecosystems.

questions.question: What is water called when it flows over land into streams or rivers?
questions.modelAnswer: Water flowing over land is runoff.

questions.question: What is an aquifer?
questions.modelAnswer: An aquifer is an underground layer that stores water and allows it to flow.

questions.question: Why does pavement often increase runoff?
questions.modelAnswer: Pavement is impermeable, so water cannot easily infiltrate and more water flows over the surface.

questions.question: Which design would most likely reduce runoff?
questions.modelAnswer: A rain garden would help hold water and increase infiltration.

questions.question: What evidence could show that a city design reduces flooding?
questions.modelAnswer: Evidence could include lower runoff measurements, less storm drain flow, higher infiltration, or fewer flooded streets after similar storms.

data.sourcePassage: Oceans cover most of Earth’s surface and store a huge amount of thermal energy. Water has a high heat capacity, so it warms and cools slowly. This helps coastal areas have milder temperatures than inland areas at similar latitude. Oceans also move heat and matter through currents. Surface currents are mainly driven by wind and can carry warm or cool water across large distances. Deep currents are mainly driven by density differences. Temperature and salinity affect density: cold water is usually denser than warm water, and saltier water is denser than fresher water. Cold, salty water can sink and help drive deep ocean circulation. Ocean temperatures, currents, salinity, sea level, sea ice, and weather data help scientists study climate patterns.

questions.question: What mainly drives surface ocean currents?
questions.modelAnswer: Surface currents are mainly driven by wind.

questions.question: What mainly drives deep ocean currents?
questions.modelAnswer: Deep currents are mainly driven by density differences.

questions.question: How do temperature and salinity affect ocean water density?
questions.modelAnswer: Cold water is usually denser than warm water, and saltier water is denser than fresher water.

questions.question: Why can coastal areas have milder temperatures than inland areas?
questions.modelAnswer: Ocean water warms and cools slowly because of high heat capacity, so it can cool summers and warm winters near coasts.

questions.question: Why do scientists need several kinds of ocean and weather data to study climate?
questions.modelAnswer: Climate is a long-term system, so scientists compare patterns in ocean temperature, currents, salinity, sea level, sea ice, and weather over time.

data.sourcePassage: Human activities can change the water cycle and ocean systems. Paving land can increase runoff and reduce infiltration. Pumping groundwater for cities and farms can lower aquifer levels if water is removed faster than it is recharged. Removing forests can change transpiration and increase runoff. Pollution can move through rivers and oceans, harming ecosystems. Greenhouse gases can affect temperature, evaporation, ice melt, sea level, and climate patterns. Scientists and engineers use evidence to understand problems and test solutions. A fair test changes one main variable at a time, measures a dependent variable, and keeps controlled variables the same. Useful evidence can include rainfall data, runoff measurements, groundwater levels, pumping rates, soil moisture, streamflow, and long-term climate records.

questions.question: Which human activity can increase runoff?
questions.modelAnswer: Paving land can increase runoff.

questions.question: What can happen if groundwater is pumped faster than it is recharged?
questions.modelAnswer: Aquifer levels can fall, wells can dry up, and water supply can become less sustainable.

questions.question: Why are controlled variables important in a fair test?
questions.modelAnswer: Controlled variables help make sure the results are due to the independent variable rather than other changing factors.

questions.question: Name two kinds of evidence that could help study groundwater sustainability.
questions.modelAnswer: Useful evidence includes rainfall data, groundwater levels, pumping rates, streamflow, soil moisture, and long-term climate records.

questions.question: Explain how human choices can affect both people and ecosystems through the water cycle.
questions.modelAnswer: Choices such as paving, pumping groundwater, removing forests, or polluting water can change runoff, infiltration, aquifer levels, streamflow, and water quality, affecting water supplies and habitats.
